appraisal_events.evidence: Swann's love dies without his being able to witness it — « bientôt l'obscurité se faisant dans son cerveau, il ne voyait plus rien, renonçait à regarder », « l'incuriosité, dans l'engourdissement du voyageur ensommeillé » — and the dream that follows stages him in a nightshirt, stared at by Mme Verdurin, left behind by Odette who « prenait congé de tout le monde, de la même façon, sans prendre à part Swann », told by le peintre of Forcheville-Napoléon III that « Elle est sa maîtresse », while « son cœur battait horriblement » and he ends in nausea and a tocsin.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator organizes the whole passage around Swann's diminishment: he loses his love without even managing to look at it, and the closing dream dramatizes his exclusion, sartorial humiliation, supplanting by Forcheville, and self-division into two dream figures. The narrator's own similes and the flat correction « Il se trompait » make this a guided, not merely reported, lowering.

appraisal_events.evidence: « une vision de haute vie qui remplit l'omnibus, mêlée à l'odeur du teinturier », « Swann se sentit déborder de tendresse pour elle », « Mme Cottard, meilleur thérapeute que n'eût été son mari, avait greffé à côté d'eux d'autres sentiments, normaux ceux-là, de gratitude, d'amitié ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The opening movement raises Mme Cottard: she wins Swann's overflowing tenderness, is credited with a real curative effect on him, and is explicitly ranked above her doctor husband — though the narrator's comic touches (the dry-cleaner's smell against the vision of high life, the aigrette held high) keep the elevation affectionately ironized.

status_effects.explanation: Swann ends locally low: his love lapses without his being able to see or say goodbye to it, and the dream leaves him snubbed, jealous-hateful, supplanted, and woken in anxiety and nausea.
She is locally raised as an object of Swann's tenderness and as an effective, sane counterweight to his morbid feeling, explicitly rated above her husband.

Forcheville is confirmed as Odette's lover both by the chance proof Swann picks up and by the dream's Napoléon III, and Swann's own dream words — « C'était bien l'homme qui pouvait la comprendre » — concede him the place Swann has vacated.

ambiguities: The extinction of Swann's love is double-valued: it ends his suffering and opens the prospect of « cette Odette aimée d'affection paisible » near whom « il pourrait vivre heureux », yet it is narrated through blindness, torpor, incuriosity, regret at not having been warned, and a culminating nightmare. Read here as dominantly diminishing, since relief is a passing note while the body of the passage and its culmination are governed by loss, exclusion and anxiety rather than by any narrator-endorsed renewal.

The dream figure named Napoléon III is explicitly glossed by the narrator as Forcheville (« en réalité... c'était bien Forcheville »); the discrediting/supplanting appraisal is therefore attached to Forcheville rather than to the historical name under which the dream presents him.
